h1:
Bun Phawet Festival Trip Plan
Roi Et's Big March Merit-Making Event
intro: If there's one event that brings the whole province of Roi Et home at the same time, it's Bun Phawet — the province's signature merit-making festival held every year in early March around Bueng Phlan Chai in the city center. There's a Phra Uppakhut procession, the 13-chapter Mahachat sermon that runs all day, and free khao pun (rice noodles) handed out to everyone who comes to make merit. We've put together a 3-day, 2-night plan so you catch the whole festival — the pre-dawn rites and the daytime processions — with restaurants and city sights worked in at a pace that won't wear you out.

blocks.html: Bun Phawet is the third-to-fourth-month merit ceremony in the Isan tradition of Heet Sip Song (the twelve monthly rites). The name "Phawet" is a local shift from "Phra Wes," or Phra Wessandon (Prince Vessantara). The festival is about hearing the whole Vessantara Jataka preached in a single day — it's believed that anyone who hears all 13 chapters earns great merit. Roi Et has run this as its provincial signature festival since 1991, held at Somdet Phra Sri Nakharin Park and the island in the middle of Bueng Phlan Chai in the heart of the city.

The festival usually falls in early March and runs for 3 days (for example, 2025 was held on 7–9 March, while 2024 was 15–17 March). The dates shift with the lunar calendar, so before you book bus tickets or a place to stay, double-check that year's dates with the Roi Et provincial PR page — accommodation around the lake fills up fast during the festival.

Before we get into the plan, here's a quick rundown of the main ceremonies, because each one happens at a different time of day. Knowing the order helps you catch the right moments for photos and for joining in.

items: Phra Uppakhut procession — the opening rite, inviting Phra Uppakhut up from the water at Bueng Phlan Chai. Belief holds that he protects the merit-making from any disturbance by Mara. It's usually held in the evening of the first day or in the pre-dawn hours of the next.
Khao Phan Kon procession — a procession carrying a thousand balls of sticky rice as an offering, done in the pre-dawn hours, symbolizing the thousand verses of the Vessantara Jataka.

Thousand-verse chant + the 13-chapter Mahachat sermon — the heart of the festival. Monks preach the Vessantara story chapter by chapter from morning to evening, while locals sit and listen and offer support for each chapter.

The 13-chapter Phawet procession — the festival's biggest parade. Each district forms a procession based on a chapter of the Jataka, in period costume, with figures like Madri, Kanha, Chali, and the Paccaya Naga elephant, circling the lake.
Khao pun (rice noodles) — free kitchens serve khao pun with curry sauce throughout the festival, in keeping with the local saying "eat khao pun, earn Phawet merit" — the thing people look forward to.

blocks.title: How to time your days
blocks.html: The most photogenic rite is the 13-chapter Phawet procession, which is usually on the festival's second day. The most moving one is the Khao Phan Kon procession in the pre-dawn hours. If you want both, arrive in Roi Et by the evening of opening day.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Arrive in Roi Et, catch the opening rite by the lake

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Settle into town, soak up the evening festival mood

items.activity: Arrive in Roi Et and check in to a place around Bueng Phlan Chai
items.note: Pick somewhere within walking distance of the lake — it's a huge help during the festival, since roads around the lake close and traffic backs up. Book several weeks ahead.

items.activity: Stroll around Bueng Phlan Chai and watch the booths and processions being set up
items.note: Bueng Phlan Chai is an island public park in the middle of the city, with the city pillar shrine and a pair of naga statues to pay respects to before you start the trip.

items.activity: Watch the Phra Uppakhut procession as the image is brought up from the lake, officially opening the festival
items.note: This opening rite draws fewer people than the big procession day, so it's easy to photograph, and you get to see the real roots of the festival's beliefs.

items.activity: Have dinner at a lakeside restaurant, then head to the walking street or cultural grounds at the festival
items.note: During Bun Phawet there's usually a stage with mor lam performances and local food around Somdet Park.

blocks.html: Today is the main day of the festival. Get up early to catch the pre-dawn rites, then rest at midday before coming back for the Phawet procession in the late morning. You'll be walking a lot today — wear comfortable shoes and bring a hat and water, because the March sun in Roi Et is strong.

items.activity: Join the Khao Phan Kon procession and the morning alms-giving at the festival grounds
items.note: The pre-dawn air is cool and pleasant, and this is when locals genuinely come to make merit — calm and full of devotion. Bring sticky rice or flowers to join the alms-giving if you like.

items.activity: Eat khao pun with curry sauce at the free kitchen on the grounds
items.note: Khao pun is the Isan style of rice noodles, handed out free by tradition, eaten with fresh vegetables and chilies — a breakfast that fills you up and earns merit at the same time.

items.activity: Sit in on the Mahachat sermon and hear the thousand-verse chant and the early chapters of the Vessantara Jataka
items.note: You don't have to hear every chapter — just sit and take in the atmosphere and the Isan chanting style for a while and you'll get the feel of it.

items.activity: Head out to watch the 13-chapter Phawet procession circle the lake
items.note: This is the photo highlight of the festival. Each district dresses its procession after a chapter of the Jataka, with the Paccaya Naga elephant, Madri, Kanha, and Chali. Grab a spot along the route early for a good angle.

items.activity: Break for lunch — find an Isan restaurant in town to sit out of the sun
items.note: See the recommended restaurants in the next section. Most are within a 10-minute drive of the lake.

items.activity: Rest your legs at a lakeside cafe and take in the afternoon festival mood
items.note: The afternoon sun softens and people start coming back out, so it's a good time to walk around and photograph the booths and local souvenirs.

items.activity: Pay respects at Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkol (if you have time and a car), or keep enjoying the festival into the evening
items.note: Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkol is in Nong Phok district, about 80 km from town. The round trip takes a while, so if your day is packed, save it for Day 3 instead.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Take it easy around town before heading home

items.activity: Give morning alms by the lake, or have breakfast Roi Et style
items.note: Rice porridge and congee shops in town open early — an easy, gentle way to wrap up a merit-making trip.

items.activity: Go up Ho Wot 101 for a high view over the city of Roi Et
items.note: Ho Wot is a city-view tower shaped like a wot (an Isan musical instrument), with viewpoints and a glass floor — you can see Bueng Phlan Chai and the whole city layout.

items.activity: Pay respects at Wat Burapha Phiram and see the tallest standing Buddha image in Thailand
items.note: Phra Phuttha Rattana Mongkol Maha Muni at Wat Burapha Phiram stands over 59 meters tall, right in town — an easy stop.

items.activity: Have a farewell lunch, then buy some local souvenirs
items.note: Popular Roi Et souvenirs are Thung Kula Ronghai jasmine rice and local silk, easy to find at souvenir shops in town.
If you're flying out, Roi Et Airport is about 13 km from town. Allow extra travel time during the festival, since there's more traffic than usual.

blocks.text: Where to eat around the festival — restaurants near Bueng Phlan Chai

blocks.html: During the festival, restaurants around the lake get packed, so plan extra time or eat outside the main meal rush. These are the places locals and reviews mention often — just pick whatever style you're in the mood for.

items.name: Tara Pub & Restaurant
items.blurb: A relaxed Thai–Isan spot right on Bueng Phlan Chai, great for catching the cool evening breeze — perfect for dinner after a full day at the festival. The menu covers everything from full dishes to small plates.
items.meta: 98/8 Nai Mueang Subdistrict · lakeside, Bueng Phlan Chai · open 10:00–24:00

items.name: Rim Huai Nuea Restaurant
items.blurb: A spacious place with several seating zones and a shady, easygoing feel — good for groups or families during a midday break.

items.name: Tam Kathoey
items.blurb: A som tam spot people in Roi Et recommend often, with plenty of styles and bold, fully loaded flavors — great for lunch if you like punchy Isan food.

items.name: Khao Tom Liang Heng
items.blurb: The standout is the free-range chicken soup fragrant with lemon basil, served by the pot, alongside crispy fried free-range chicken — good for a late dinner after the festival or a filling breakfast.
items.meta: in town · rice soup–free-range chicken soup

items.name: Free khao pun kitchen at the festival
items.blurb: The must-try of Bun Phawet — khao pun (rice noodles) with curry sauce, handed out free by tradition. Easy to eat while you walk between ceremonies, filling and full of merit.
items.meta: festival grounds, Somdet Park–Bueng Phlan Chai · free

blocks.title: About where to stay
blocks.html: There aren't many places to stay within walking distance of Bueng Phlan Chai, and they fill up fast during the festival. If you can't get an inner spot, try the area just outside, a 5–10 minute drive away, and use your own car or a ride-hail, since some roads around the lake close during the festival.

blocks.text: What to prepare before Bun Phawet

items: Check that year's dates — the festival shifts with the lunar calendar, so check the Roi Et provincial PR page before buying tickets and booking a room.
Dress modestly — this is a merit-making event at temples and public parks, so wear sleeved tops and knee-covering pants or skirts. Thai-style fabric fits right in.
Come early on procession day — the 13-chapter Phawet procession draws big crowds, so claim a spot along the route early for good photos.
Prepare for the sun — the March sun in Roi Et is strong, so carry a hat, sunglasses, water, and sunscreen.
Bring cash — the free kitchen is free, but souvenirs, festival food, and many local shops are easier to handle in cash.

faq.q: What month and dates is the Bun Phawet Festival in Roi Et?
faq.a: It's held in early March every year and runs for 3 days, with dates shifting by the lunar calendar — for example, 2025 was 7–9 March and 2024 was 15–17 March. Before planning, check that year's dates again with the Roi Et provincial PR office.

faq.q: Where in Roi Et is it held?
faq.a: It's held at Somdet Phra Sri Nakharin Park Roi Et and the island in the middle of Bueng Phlan Chai, right in the heart of Roi Et city — they're within walking distance of each other, so staying around the lake is the most convenient.

faq.q: Which ceremonies should I see at Bun Phawet?
faq.a: The highlights are the 13-chapter Phawet procession, usually on the festival's second day, and the pre-dawn rites like the Khao Phan Kon procession and alms-giving. If you want to understand the roots of the festival, catch the Phra Uppakhut procession on opening day.

faq.q: Do I have to pay for the khao pun at the festival?
faq.a: No. Khao pun (rice noodles) is handed out free at the festival kitchens, in keeping with the saying "eat khao pun, earn Phawet merit" — it's a must-try of the festival.

faq.q: How many days do I need for Bun Phawet?
faq.a: 2 days and 1 night is enough to catch the main ceremonies, but if you want the pre-dawn rites, the daytime procession, and time to explore Roi Et city too, 3 days and 2 nights is just right — not too rushed.
